name: Colin Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Colin, thanks for this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I've done a couple of surveys before but never a proper chat like this. Fire away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the home farm of the Ashdown estate, which is owned by a family who live in the city and visit twice a year. The farm manager, Graham, runs it day to day: about four hundred outdoor pigs, plus wheat and oilseed rape. My day is mostly pigs, so feeding, checking the arcs, moving electric fences, sorting weaners, and then tractor work at harvest. I've been there three years and I'm still the one who gets the muddiest jobs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pigs, they're cleverer than people think and they've all got their own moods. The hard bit is the pay, which is the bottom of the scale, and the rented cottage in the village eats half of it. My partner Mira drives the school bus, so between us we manage, but we've got maybe two weeks of money spare. One broken boiler and we're done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI just becomes a slightly better tool and that's it. Honestly, part of me would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because there's a lot of hot air about AI. I'd probably joke at the pub that the estate still needs someone to chase escaped sows across the road. Online I'd maybe share something about how the money went to tech bosses and not to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much shifts, and that's the problem as much as the comfort. I'm still on the lowest rate, still renting from a landlord who puts it up every April. The farm is fine, the job's fine, but fine on this pay doesn't get Mira and me a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ashdown and keep using the chat app now and then, like I did when the weaners had scours and I wanted a second opinion before ringing the vet. I'd ask Graham about the pig unit qualification the estate half promised me. And I'd keep pushing the union rep about the pay scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, a bit flat about everything else. It's the same treadmill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Graham about a qualification. What is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a stockperson certificate, about six months of day-release at the agricultural college. It would bump my rate up a grade. Graham said yes last year and then nothing happened, so I'd push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the April rent rise do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year it went up forty a month and that came straight out of what we'd been saving. Mira did extra trips on the summer holiday runs to cover it. Every April our landlord takes the bit of savings Mira (his partner) and I managed to scrape together over the winter.

say: I'd say AI was mostly **hot air** all along.
I'd say the gains went to **tech bosses**, not workers.
think: My **job is safe**, but my pay still doesn't build a future.
The **April rent rise** keeps eating what Mira and I save.
do: Keep using the **chat app** for second opinions before ringing the vet.
Push Graham for the **stockperson certificate** the estate promised.
Keep pressing the **union rep** about the pay scale.
feel: **Relieved** about the job, flat about the money.
Stuck on the same **treadmill** as before.
S0.quote: Every April our landlord takes the bit of savings Mira (his partner) and I managed to scrape together over the winter.
fieldNote: Colin sees AI as a **useful second opinion**, nothing more, in this picture.
His real pressure is **rent and low pay**, which AI Plateau doesn't change.
He blames **landlords and pay scales** rather than his own employer.

steps.text: Keep working the outdoor pig unit at Ashdown
Push Graham to fund the six-month stockperson certificate
Press the union rep to raise the farm pay scale

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots slowly into hands-on work. Graham's already been to a show looking at automatic feeders, so that's not imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules, like any big change does. If the estate saves money with machines, some of that should go to the people who did the work before. I'd say it at union meetings and probably on the local farming group online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the estate would cut a post and it might be mine. The office side will go to AI first, and that's Graham's paperwork, not my job. But once those feeders and the camera system that spots lame pigs are proven, a junior like me is the easy saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto that stockperson certificate within the first six months, whatever it takes. I'd start using the AI apps a bit more, the ones for pig health records, so I'm the one who knows the system. And Mira and I would stop the one weekend away we take each year and put that money aside instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's the sort of worry I can do something about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Petra, who's been on the arable side twenty years and won't touch a phone. If the estate brings in a self-steering sprayer, she'd struggle. I'd worry about her more than me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the apps more. Isn't that helping bring in the change you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But the machines are coming whether I learn them or not. I'd rather be the pig man who understands the camera than the one it replaces.

say: I'd say the change needs **rules**, like any big change.
I'd say machine savings should be **shared with workers**.
think: The office goes first, but a **junior post** like mine is the easy cut later.
Proven **automatic feeders** and lameness cameras would put me at risk.
do: Start the **stockperson certificate** within six months.
Use the **pig health apps** more so I know the system.
Skip our yearly **weekend away** and save that money.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to act on it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the pig man who understands the camera than the one it replaces.
fieldNote: Colin's steady streak shows: he'd adopt **pig-health apps** once proven around him.
He separates the office AI shift from the slower **robot threat** to his own role.
He worries about **older colleagues** like Petra more than himself.

steps.text: Enrol on the stockperson certificate within six months
Learn the pig-health record app and the lameness camera
Skip the yearly weekend away and bank the money
Post in the local farming group calling for shared savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's basically tomorrow for the estate, they plan five years at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a political choice, not the weather. Governments could tax the companies and pay people through it. I'd be at whatever rally the union organised and I'd vote for whoever said that plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the estate keeps me till the robots land in 2031 and then lets me go. The thinking AI in 2028 hits Graham before me, which is strange to picture. Mira's bus would probably go driverless around the same time, so it's both of us, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sign up for a course in farm machinery maintenance at the college, because someone has to fix the robots. I'd cut everything: phone contract down, no pub, cheaper food. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a transition fund for farm workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, the kind where you lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the thinking AI hits Graham first. What does that look like on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham spends half his day on the computer, ordering feed, pig movements, the subsidy forms. If AI does all that in 2028, the estate might not need a manager, just a remote office and me on the ground. Being the last human on the pig unit for three more years would be a strange way to turn thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, we'd share Mira's. Then the gym membership I never use anyway. Then the phone contracts go down to the cheapest. Selling the car would hurt, because I'd be cycling three miles to the estate in winter.

say: I'd say this is a **political choice**, not the weather.
I'd say governments should **tax the companies** and support people.
think: The estate keeps me until the **robots in 2031**, then lets me go.
Mira's **bus job** could go driverless too, so it's both of us.
do: Sign up for a **machinery maintenance** course straight away.
Cut the **phone contracts**, pub and food bill.
Push the union for a **transition fund** for farm workers.
S2.quote: Being the last human on the pig unit for three more years would be a strange way to turn thirty.
fieldNote: Colin uses the **three-year gap** to retrain as a robot maintainer.
He worries about **two incomes**, since Mira's bus driving is exposed too.
His blame is **political**: tax the companies and fund the change.

steps.text: Enrol on a farm machinery maintenance course at the college
Sell the car and share Mira's to save money
Push the union for a transition fund for farm workers
Vote for candidates who back taxing AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI and then 2034 for the robots. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it properly if governments start now. I'd say it on the farming group and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done. I'd be the annoying one at the union saying we need a plan, not a protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me a real shot. With eight years until robots on the pig unit, I could finish the stockperson certificate and a machinery course and be the one maintaining the kit. It still might not work, because the estate might only need one robot technician across three farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the stockperson certificate in year one and the maintenance course after. I'd start saving thirty pounds a week, which is a stretch. Mira and I would talk about whether she retrains too, maybe as a school mechanic or something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's some hope in this one. It's a ladder, even if it's a wobbly one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe only one technician across three farms. What if it isn't you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be looking further away, maybe the dealer in the market town who sells the machines. They'd need people to fit them. I don't want to move, though, we've only just got settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools to help you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd use it to quiz me on engines and hydraulics. The AI tutor is patient, and it doesn't sigh when I ask the same thing twice like the college tutor did.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if governments start now.
I'd write to **our MP** for the first time.
think: Eight years until robots gives me **a real shot** at retraining.
The estate might need **one technician** for three farms, so it might not be me.
do: Finish the **stockperson certificate** in year one.
Save **thirty pounds a week**, even though it's a stretch.
feel: **Worried** but with some hope, like a wobbly ladder.
S3.quote: The AI tutor is patient, and it doesn't sigh when I ask the same thing twice like the college tutor did.
fieldNote: Colin sees **eight years** as enough to climb into a technician role.
He'd use **AI as a tutor**, which fits his steady, practical take-up.
His fallback is the **machinery dealer**, but he doesn't want to move.

steps.text: Finish the stockperson certificate in the first year
Use an AI app to quiz himself on engines
Save thirty pounds a week from wages
Write to the local MP asking for a training plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots in 2039. That's practically a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to get it right, with proper training and shorter hours rather than layoffs. I'd say it at the union and I'd mean it. Ten years is long enough for a decent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be forty when the robots come, and I could be a skilled technician by then. The pig unit will still need someone who knows pigs for a good while. I'm more worried about whether Mira and I ever get a house than about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the courses slowly, one a year, and keep working. I'd use the AI apps more for records so I'm comfortable with them. And I'd keep pushing the union on pay, because a decade of low pay is a decade of no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're more worried about a house. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the rent rises every year. A deposit for even a small place round here is two years of Mira's (his partner's) wages, and AI doesn't change that. If anything, people with money buy up houses round here as holiday lets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what you'd say about AI at the pub?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be less grumpy about it, probably. I'd say learn it now while you've got time. Some of the older lads would roll their eyes.

say: I'd say it's a chance for **training and shorter hours**, not layoffs.
I'd say ten years is enough for a **decent plan**.
think: I could be a **skilled technician** by 2039, when I'm forty.
A **house deposit** worries me more than the robots ever will.
The pig unit will need someone who **knows pigs** for a while yet.
do: Take **one course a year** while working.
Use the **record apps** more to stay comfortable.
Keep pushing the union on **pay rates**.
S4.quote: A deposit for even a small place round here is two years of Mira's (his partner's) wages, and AI doesn't change that.
fieldNote: With a decade, Colin's worry shifts from robots back to **housing costs**.
He'd pace training at **one course a year** alongside work.
He frames AI as a chance for **shorter hours** if workers organise.

steps.text: Take one agricultural college course each year
Move pig records onto the estate's AI app
Keep pressing the union for a higher pay grade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mira and I would both be exposed and we've got two weeks of savings. What would help is a proper transition fund, paid for by the companies, that covers wages while people retrain. And a course I could do on day release without losing pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks about my job, but it's the two jobs together that keep the roof up. If both go in the same few years, that's the real disaster.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but it's the two jobs together that keep the roof up.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old pig man** on an absentee-owned estate farm, renting a village cottage with his partner Mira.
He uses **AI apps** now and then and would adopt pig-health tools once proven.
His plan in every picture is to **retrain** toward stockperson and machinery skills.
He blames **politics and landlords** and wants companies to fund transition.
His fear peaks in **AGI by 2028**, when both his and Mira's jobs look exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household jobs at risk and only two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition fund** paid by companies that covers wages during retraining.
**Day-release courses** that don't cost him pay.
